3. [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order for a point [MATH: (a,b)] to lie on the graph of the function [MATH: y=\arcsin x,] the following conditions must hold:

  • The reflected point [MATH: (b,a)] must lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.]

  • The [MATH: y]-value of the point must lie in the range of [MATH: y=\arcsin x,] which is [MATH: y\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right].]

With this in mind, let's check each of the points.

  • First, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.] [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]

  • Next, we consider the point [MATH: \left(0,\pi \right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\pi,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arcsin x] is [MATH: y\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],] and [MATH: y=\pi] does not lie within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(0,\pi\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]

  • Finally, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arcsin x] is [MATH: y\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],] and [MATH: y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] lies within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] does lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]

With this in mind, let's check each of the points.

- The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.] [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]

- Next, we consider the point [MATH: \left(0,\pi \right).] We note the following:

- The point [MATH: \left(\pi,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- The range of [MATH: y=\arcsin x] is [MATH: y\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],] and [MATH: y=\pi] does not lie within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(0,\pi\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]
- Finally, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).] We note the following:

- The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- The range of [MATH: y=\arcsin x] is [MATH: y\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],] and [MATH: y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] lies within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] does lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arcsin x.]
